doc.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Rehearsing Dizzy Gillespie's arrangements
summary: Gillespie rehearsed the band seriously, was hard on the substitute drummer, and had taught others about Afro-Cuban influence.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Yeah. And also the other thing that was exciting about that was we were playing mostly Dizzy’s, maybe entirely Dizzy’s arrangements, his old big band arrangements. And we had an extensive rehearsal with him. And having him show us how these compositions were meant to be played was really enlightening and fun. He was serious about it. He did joke around a lot, but he was serious about the music. He was especially hard on the drummer I’ll say, who was a good drummer, but there was a lot of stuff that you don’t write into the chart that you just have to know, and he could be very specific. He knew a lot about drumming and also, he was going to be filling some big shoes, stepping in for J.C. Heard. So he wanted to make sure that this guy did a good job, and he did.
Seems like I read somewhere that he even taught Art Blakey to play drums or something.

I wouldn’t doubt that he at least had some things to share when him, to help him. Because he was one of the first guys into the Afro-Cuban influence on jazz, and combining those things together. And I think he taught a lot of people stuff about that you know.
